strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear gap in existing work regarding localized, time-sensitive sequence modifications
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (WOT, eICU, MIMIC-IV), encoders (Transformer, xLSTM, MOMENT), and evaluation metrics (MAE, RMSE, R²)
Rigorous generalization testing using SPECTRA with varying train/test similarities and zero-shot evaluation
Introduction of new benchmark datasets (WOT-CF, carefully stratified patient splits) that could benefit future research
Formal problem definition with clear definitions of sequence editing, temporal concepts, and controllable editing
Case studies showing plausible physiological relationships (e.g., glucose-WBC correlation in T1D patients)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: temporal concepts are simply multiplicative factors (c = x_{:,tk}/x_{:,tj}), learned via element-wise operations and optional FNN. Architecture is an incremental wrapper around existing encoders with no deep innovation.

SimpleLinear baseline (all concepts = 1) performs competitively or better on several tasks (e.g., WOT delayed editing), contradicting claims that learned temporal concepts capture meaningful patterns and regularize effectively.

Core technical design poorly justified: multiplicative decoding (Eq. 2) is overly restrictive, assumes uniform scaling across variables, prevents value decrease, and forces linear growth assumptions. No justification for why multiplication vs. other operations.

Causality claims unsupported: patient data is observational (no true interventions), transcription factors in cellular data are inferred not measured. Paper acknowledges need for 'real-world causal model' but frames work as causal reasoning without it.

Case study validation is circular: manually reducing glucose (a disease marker) then verifying result resembles healthy patients is tautological. Indirect effects (WBC reduction) lack rigorous validation; clinical applicability is overstated.

Weak baselines and confounded comparisons: VAR fails catastrophically (MAE 55982.74), suggesting misconfiguration; CLEF only tested as wrapper around other encoders; no direct comparison to recent conditional generation methods cited (Jing et al. 2024, Bao et al. 2024).

Dataset limitations: WOT uses synthetic simulations with inferred conditions; patient data lacks interventional ground truth for validating counterfactuals; zero-shot setup with predetermined divergence time is artificial.

Hyperparameter sensitivity undermines core claims: optimal FNN layers vary by dataset (0 for WOT, 1 for eICU/MIMIC-IV), suggesting learned nonlinearity may not be necessary and temporal concept learning claim is questionable.
MOMENT encoder consistently underperforms across all datasets despite being a foundation model, suggesting approach benefits are encoder-dependent and may not generalize.

No interpretability analysis: no visualization of learned concepts, no demonstration of what concepts capture, no analysis of failure modes. Manual concept intervention in case studies is trajectory engineering, not interpretation.

strengths: Clearly articulates an important limitation in existing sequence editing methods: lack of control over intervention timing and scope. Well-motivated clinical examples make the problem concrete.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 diverse datasets with 9 SOTA baselines, multiple evaluation protocols (standard splits, SPECTRA-based generalization), and proper ablations isolating temporal concepts' contribution.

Strong empirical results with consistent improvements: 16.28% on immediate editing, 26.73% on delayed editing, up to 62.84% on counterfactual generation. Demonstrates better generalization to unseen patient trajectories.
Fair experimental design where CLEF and non-CLEF models differ only in concept encoder/decoder, enabling proper attribution of performance gains to the proposed contribution.
Interpretable and intervenable temporal concepts (per-variable scalars) enable direct user intervention for hypothesis exploration, demonstrated convincingly in T1D case studies.
Architectural flexibility: framework works with multiple sequence encoders (Transformer, xLSTM, MOMENT). Can be integrated into existing conditional generation and counterfactual prediction models.
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendices with experimental setup, hyperparameters, implementation details, code release promised, and four new benchmark datasets released.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core architecture is straightforward (element-wise multiplication + optional FFN + GELU). Design choices (why these operations? why GELU?) lack justification. More engineering contribution than algorithmic insight.

Weak theoretical foundation for counterfactual claims. Assumption 3.4 assumes learned concepts capture 'balanced' representations but provides no explicit enforcement mechanism. Connection between architecture (Eq. 2) and balanced representations is stated but never proven. Marginal empirical support via BCE loss (Tables 10-12).

Temporal concept limitations: multiplicative model (Definition 3.2) enforces linearity, cannot capture additive offsets or discontinuous changes. Per-variable scalar concepts prevent capturing cross-variable dependencies and hierarchical patterns. Paper acknowledges but doesn't adequately address implications.

Experimental setup concerns: (1) Baseline methods (Transformer, xLSTM) designed for next-step prediction may not be optimized for arbitrary future forecasting. (2) VAR shows implausibly extreme errors (MAE 10^23-10^39) on patient data with no explanation provided. (3) WOT data simulated from optimal transport model, not biological reality. (4) Patient data heavily preprocessed with 80% filtering.

Insufficient clinical validation of case studies: Only 59/25 T1D patients in eICU/MIMIC respectively. Manual interventions (0.5x, 2x glucose) are arbitrary. R² similarity to healthy controls is indirect proxy for plausibility. No physician review of whether counterfactuals are medically sensible or clinically actionable.

Temporal concept interpretability not validated: No analysis of whether learned concepts match domain knowledge or have clinical significance. Table 5 shows concepts preserve unedited variables but doesn't explain what patterns emerge or their meaning.

Causal assumptions insufficiently addressed: Paper doesn't discuss sensitivity to unobserved confounding, a critical concern for observational EHR data. Footnote 1 assumes conditions occur 'shortly before' measurements, which is often violated clinically.

Missing comparisons: Several relevant methods excluded due to unavailable code (CF-GODE, Causal CPC, Mamba-CDSP). No comparison to recent diffusion-based conditional generation or neural ODE approaches for longitudinal data.
